newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Voting begins in cliffhanger New Zealand election.
newsitem.headline: Voting begins in cliffhanger New Zealand election.

text.p: Voters rushed to polls in New Zealand on Saturday in what was forecast to be a knife-edge contest in the first election under a new proportional system.
Queues formed at polling booths and returning officers reported a steady stream of voters.
They have a choice of 21 parties ranging from the Natural Law Party advocating yogic flying to the pro-marijuna Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party and the McGillicuddy Serious Party.
However, pre-election polls suggest a tight contest between the ruling conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party, backed by the more left-wing Alliance Party.
Deputy Chief Electoral Officer Hugh Garland doubted many would be put off by possible poor weather. "It's an historic occasion. People will want to be involved."
Chief Electoral Officer Phil Whelan said 92 percent of 2.4 million eligible voters had registered and early indications were there would be a high poll.
Polls close at 7.00 p.m. (0600 GMT) with counting expected to be completed four hours later.
Unlike under the former first-past-the-post system, a clear decision on who rules may not be known for weeks. A government will only be agreed after complex negotiations.

The last pre-election poll suggested National with its probable allies -- the radical free-market Act New Zealand and the centrist United Party -- will have 50 seats in the expanded 120 seat parliament.
That number would be precisely matched by Labour and the Alliance, leaving New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, a charismatic Maori, as kingmaker with his party's 20 seats.
Peters has hinted his party will back Labour leader Helen Clark in her bid to be the country's first woman prime minister.
But he has kept his options open, campaigning for more open and accountable government and limits on foreign ownership, particularly of "strategic" assets.
Issues came second to coalition bargaining during the lacklustre five-week campaign.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger said the election was a choice between the stable orthodox economic policies of the past six years, which have brought growth and jobs, and leftist plans to roll back free market reforms.

Clark, thought by commentators to have ran a flawless campaign hugely increasing her personal and party's standing, said the election was about spreading the fruits of New Zealand's economic recovery more evenly.
She promises to spend more on education and health, paid for by higher taxes on the well-off.

Bolger has seen a 20 point lead over Labour earlier this year shrink to four points by this week. He has attempted to rally flagging support by suggesting Labour was teaming up with "old fashioned socialists".
